items.stem: Which is a function of money?
items.answer: A store of value
items.markingKey: Functions: medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value, standard of deferred payment.

items.stem: Explain the problems of a barter economy and how money overcomes them.
items.answer: Barter needs a double coincidence of wants, has no common measure of value, and goods may be indivisible or perishable. Money is a medium of exchange, a unit of account and a store of value, reducing transaction costs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: double coincidence; 1 mark: other problem; 1 mark: money’s functions [3]

items.stem: Explain two characteristics that an item must have to function well as money.
items.answer: Acceptability, durability, portability, divisibility, homogeneity, limited supply (scarcity), difficult to counterfeit.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each identified, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: Data for Selmaria ($ billion): notes and coins in circulation 40; sight deposits 500; time deposits 900; certificates of deposit 100; commercial banks’ reserves at the central bank 20. Calculate narrow money (cash plus sight deposits).
items.answer: $540 billion

items.stem: Data for Ostrelia ($ billion): notes and coins in circulation 80; sight deposits 600; time deposits 1200; certificates of deposit 80; commercial banks’ reserves at the central bank 40. Calculate narrow money (cash plus sight deposits) and broad money (narrow money plus time deposits and CDs). Explain why central banks monitor broad money.
items.answer: Narrow = $680 billion; broad = $1960 billion. Broad money reflects spending power and credit creation that can feed through to aggregate demand and inflation.
items.markingKey: Narrow 80 + 600 [1]; broad 680 + 1200 + 80 [1]; banks’ reserves are not part of the money supply held by the public [1]; reason [1].

items.stem: Extract: Broad money in Gorvania grew by 15% last year after the central bank cut its policy rate to 0.5% and began buying government bonds. Inflation is 4% and real GDP growth is 1.5%. Some economists warn of future inflation; others say velocity has fallen. (a) Using the quantity theory, estimate the change in velocity implied by the data. (b) Explain two functions of the central bank shown in the extract.
items.answer: (a) %ΔV ≈ %ΔP + %ΔY − %ΔM = 4 + 1.5 − 15 = -9.5% (b) Monetary policy (setting rates, QE), banker to government (bond market), lender of last resort.

items.stem: Most payments in Marvona are now made by mobile phone rather than cash. Explain whether these balances count as money.
items.answer: Yes: balances that can be spent immediately are generally accepted as a medium of exchange, so they form part of narrow (or broad) money, like sight deposits.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: accepted medium of exchange; 1 mark: classification [2]

items.stem: Data for Gorvania ($ billion): notes and coins in circulation 60; sight deposits 600; time deposits 1200; certificates of deposit 50; commercial banks’ reserves at the central bank 20. Calculate narrow money (cash plus sight deposits).
items.answer: $660 billion

items.stem: If banks keep a reserve ratio of 10%, the credit multiplier is
items.markingKey: Credit multiplier = 1 / reserve ratio = 1/0.1.

items.stem: Explain why the actual credit multiplier is usually smaller than 1 / reserve ratio.
items.answer: Some money leaks out as cash held by the public; banks may hold excess reserves; there may be too few creditworthy borrowers; capital requirements limit lending.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each leakage/limit explained [2]

items.stem: Explain the conflict between liquidity and profitability for a commercial bank.
items.answer: Liquid assets (cash, reserves, short-term bills) earn little; profitable assets (long-term loans) cannot quickly be turned into cash. Banks must balance meeting withdrawals against earning returns.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: liquid but low return; 1 mark: profitable but illiquid; 1 mark: balance [3]

items.stem: Banks in Halvoria keep 5% of deposits as reserves. A new deposit of $200 million is made. Calculate the maximum total increase in deposits.
items.answer: $4000 million
items.markingKey: Multiplier = 1/0.05 = 20; ΔDeposits = 200 × 20 = 4000.

items.stem: A customer deposits $500 million in a bank in Nordavia. All banks keep a reserve ratio of 5% and lend the rest, which is re-deposited. (a) Show the first three rounds of deposits, reserves and loans. (b) Calculate the credit multiplier, the maximum increase in total deposits and new loans created. (c) Calculate the effect if the reserve ratio doubles.
items.answer: (a) deposit 500, reserve 25, loan 475; deposit 475, reserve 23.75, loan 451.25; deposit 451.25, reserve 22.56, loan 428.69 (b) multiplier 20; deposits $10,000m; loans $9500m (c) multiplier 10; deposits $5000m.
items.markingKey: (a) each round: reserve = rr × deposit, loan re-deposited [2]; (b) 1/rr, deposits = initial × multiplier, loans = deposits − initial [2]; (c) multiplier halves [1].

items.stem: A customer deposits $500 million in a bank in Quentara. All banks keep a reserve ratio of 8% and lend the rest, which is re-deposited. (a) Show the first three rounds of deposits, reserves and loans. (b) Calculate the credit multiplier, the maximum increase in total deposits and new loans created. (c) Calculate the effect if the reserve ratio doubles.
items.answer: (a) deposit 500, reserve 40, loan 460; deposit 460, reserve 36.8, loan 423.2; deposit 423.2, reserve 33.86, loan 389.34 (b) multiplier 12.5; deposits $6250m; loans $5750m (c) multiplier 6.25; deposits $3125m.
items.markingKey: (a) each round: reserve = rr × deposit, loan re-deposited [2]; (b) 1/rr, deposits = initial × multiplier, loans = deposits − initial [2]; (c) multiplier halves [1].

items.stem: Extract: Broad money in Lunaria grew by 15% last year after the central bank cut its policy rate to 0.5% and began buying government bonds. Inflation is 6% and real GDP growth is 1.5%. Some economists warn of future inflation; others say velocity has fallen. (a) Explain how bond purchases by the central bank increase the money supply. (b) Explain two functions of the central bank shown in the extract.
items.answer: (a) Central bank pays with new reserves; banks’ reserves and deposits rise; credit multiplier. (b) Monetary policy (setting rates, QE), banker to government (bond market), lender of last resort.

items.stem: Extract: Broad money in Rovania grew by 15% last year after the central bank cut its policy rate to 0.5% and began buying government bonds. Inflation is 3% and real GDP growth is 1.5%. Some economists warn of future inflation; others say velocity has fallen. (a) Using liquidity preference theory, explain why lower interest rates may not raise spending much. (b) Explain two functions of the central bank shown in the extract.
items.answer: (a) Liquidity trap: at very low rates people hold extra money rather than bonds; low confidence. (b) Monetary policy (setting rates, QE), banker to government (bond market), lender of last resort.

items.stem: Banks in Umbria Nova became very cautious after a financial crisis and held large excess reserves. Explain the effect on the credit multiplier.
items.answer: Excess reserves mean less of each deposit is lent out, so the actual multiplier falls well below 1/required reserve ratio and credit creation slows.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: less lending; 1 mark: smaller multiplier [2]

items.markingKey: (a) each round: reserve = rr × deposit, loan re-deposited [2]; (b) 1/rr, deposits = initial × multiplier, loans = deposits − initial [2]; (c) multiplier halves [1].

items.stem: Acting as lender of last resort means that the central bank
options: lends to commercial banks that face a shortage of liquidity
items.answer: lends to commercial banks that face a shortage of liquidity
items.markingKey: Prevents bank runs and financial crises.

items.stem: Open market operations involve the central bank
options: buying or selling government securities to influence the money supply and interest rates
items.answer: buying or selling government securities to influence the money supply and interest rates
items.markingKey: Buying bonds injects reserves (expansionary).

items.stem: Explain how a central bank can use open market operations to reduce the money supply.
items.answer: It sells government bonds; buyers pay with bank deposits, reducing commercial banks’ reserves at the central bank, which limits their ability to lend and pushes up interest rates.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: sells bonds; 1 mark: reserves fall; 1 mark: less lending/higher rates [3]

items.stem: The central bank of Merania raises banks’ minimum reserve requirement from 8% to 12%. Analyse the effect on the money supply.
items.answer: Credit multiplier falls from 12.5 to about 8.3, so for a given reserve base banks can support fewer deposits; lending and broad money fall; interest rates on loans rise.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: multiplier values; 1 mark: less lending; 1 mark: money supply falls; 1 mark: interest rates [4]

items.stem: The government of Rovania is considering giving its central bank full independence. Consider whether an independent central bank is essential for controlling inflation.
items.answer: Arguments for: Independence gives credibility and anchors expectations. Arguments against / evaluation: Supply shocks, fiscal policy and global factors affect inflation; accountability concerns; some dependent central banks succeed. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.

items.stem: Extract: Broad money in Ostrelia grew by 20% last year after the central bank cut its policy rate to 0.5% and began buying government bonds. Inflation is 4% and real GDP growth is 1.5%. Some economists warn of future inflation; others say velocity has fallen. (a) Using the quantity theory, estimate the change in velocity implied by the data. (b) Explain how bond purchases by the central bank increase the money supply.
items.answer: (a) %ΔV ≈ %ΔP + %ΔY − %ΔM = 4 + 1.5 − 20 = -14.5% (b) Central bank pays with new reserves; banks’ reserves and deposits rise; credit multiplier.

items.stem: The quantity theory of money is based on the equation
items.answer: MV = PY (or MV = PT)
items.markingKey: Fisher equation of exchange.

items.stem: With the aid of a diagram, explain how the interest rate is determined in liquidity preference theory.
items.answer: Diagram: interest rate on vertical axis, quantity of money on horizontal; money supply vertical (set by central bank); liquidity preference (money demand) curve downward sloping, flattening at low rates (liquidity trap). Equilibrium rate where Ms = L. An increase in Ms lowers the rate unless in the liquidity trap.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: vertical Ms; 1 mark: downward L curve; 1 mark: equilibrium and shift [3]

items.stem: Explain why the quantity theory of money may not hold in the short run.
items.answer: Velocity is not constant (it changes with confidence and financial innovation) and output may rise when there is spare capacity, so money growth may raise Y rather than P.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: V varies; 1 mark: Y can change [2]

items.stem: In Lunaria, the money supply is $250 billion, the velocity of circulation is 6 and real output is 500 billion units. Calculate the price level using MV = PY.

In Westaria, MV = PY with M = $250 billion, V = 5 and Y = 500 billion units. (a) Calculate the price level. (b) Next year the money supply grows by 12%, velocity changes by -2% and real output grows by 2%. Calculate the inflation rate.
items.answer: (a) P = 2.5 (b) inflation = 7.61% (approximately 12 + (-2) − 2 = 8%).

items.stem: In Korvia, MV = PY with M = $200 billion, V = 6 and Y = 500 billion units. (a) Calculate the price level. (b) Next year the money supply grows by 12%, velocity changes by 2% and real output grows by 3%. Calculate the inflation rate. (c) A perpetual bond pays $4 a year and its price changes from $50 to $62.5. Calculate the yield before and after and explain the link with liquidity preference.
items.answer: (a) P = 2.4 (b) inflation = 10.91% (approximately 12 + (2) − 3 = 11%). (c) Yield = 8% then 6.4%; bond prices and interest rates move inversely, so expectations of rising rates (falling bond prices) increase the speculative demand for money.
items.markingKey: (a) MV/Y [1]; (b) (1 + 12%)(1 + 2%)/(1 + 3%) − 1 = 10.91% [2]; approximation accepted [1]. (c) yield = coupon/price × 100 each [1]; inverse relationship and speculative motive [1].

items.stem: Explain the three motives for holding money in liquidity preference theory.
items.answer: Transactions (day-to-day spending, depends on income); precautionary (unexpected needs, depends on income); speculative (holding money instead of bonds, inversely related to the interest rate).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [3]

items.stem: Interest rates in Ostrelia are expected to rise next year. Explain the effect on the speculative demand for money.
items.answer: Expected rate rises imply falling bond prices; holding bonds risks capital losses, so people hold more money: speculative demand rises.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: bond prices fall; 1 mark: hold money [2]

items.stem: Money acting as a unit of account means that it
options: provides a common measure of the value of goods and services
can be used to repay debts in the future
items.answer: provides a common measure of the value of goods and services
items.markingKey: Prices expressed in money allow comparison.

items.stem: Inflation in Korvia has reached 300% a year and people are using foreign currency for many purchases. Explain which functions of money the national currency is failing to perform.
items.answer: It fails as a store of value (purchasing power falls rapidly) and increasingly as a unit of account and medium of exchange, as prices are quoted and paid in foreign currency.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: store of value; 1 mark: unit of account/medium of exchange [2]

items.stem: A growing number of shops in Halvoria accept digital currencies. To what extent do you agree that cryptocurrencies can perform all the functions of money?
items.answer: Arguments for: Some are accepted as a medium of exchange, are divisible, portable and hard to counterfeit; stablecoins aim at stable value. Arguments against / evaluation: Volatile value undermines the store of value and unit of account functions; acceptability is limited; supply and regulation are uncertain. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.

items.stem: Quantitative easing is
options: the central bank creating money to buy financial assets such as government bonds
a rise in the base rate
a reduction in the reserve ratio to zero
items.answer: the central bank creating money to buy financial assets such as government bonds
items.markingKey: Used when interest rates are near zero.

items.stem: Explain why central banks are often made independent of government.
items.answer: To remove political pressure to cut rates before elections, giving credibility to inflation targets and anchoring expectations.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: removes political short-termism; 1 mark: credibility/expectations [2]

items.stem: A bank in Valdoria faces a sudden run as depositors withdraw funds. Analyse the role the central bank might play.
items.answer: As lender of last resort, it lends to the bank against collateral so depositors can be repaid, preventing contagion to other banks; moral hazard risk if banks expect rescue; supervision role.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: lender of last resort; 1 mark: prevents contagion; 1 mark: moral hazard; 1 mark: supervision [4]

items.stem: The central bank of Selmaria has increased the money supply rapidly. (a) Explain the quantity theory of money. (b) ‘Inflation is always caused by excessive growth of the money supply.’ Evaluate this statement.

items.stem: Extract: Broad money in Zentara grew by 15% last year after the central bank cut its policy rate to 0.5% and began buying government bonds. Inflation is 4% and real GDP growth is 1.5%. Some economists warn of future inflation; others say velocity has fallen. (a) Explain how bond purchases by the central bank increase the money supply. (b) Using liquidity preference theory, explain why lower interest rates may not raise spending much.
items.answer: (a) Central bank pays with new reserves; banks’ reserves and deposits rise; credit multiplier. (b) Liquidity trap: at very low rates people hold extra money rather than bonds; low confidence.
